newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi court adjourns British nurses murder trial.
newsitem.headline: Saudi court adjourns British nurses murder trial.

text.p: A Saudi Arabian court trying two British nurses for the murder of an Australian colleague adjourned on Monday for deliberation after the victim's family insisted on the death sentence, defence lawyers said.
The law firm of Salah al-Hejailan, defending the Britons, said the three-judge court decided "to retain the case for deliberation and contemplation".
It was not known when the court would meet again.
A defence statement said the case could proceed in one of four directions including the possible sentencing of the two nurses to prison terms if found guilty.

The court may also rule that the confessions are invalid and dismiss the case or ask the public prosecutor to examine the evidence along with defence lawyers at future hearings without intervention by representatives of the victim's family.
One other option is that the court may submit the case to higher judicial authority with the court's recommendation to invalidate the confessions.

Lucille McLauchlan, 31, and Deborah Parry, 38, are facing trial for the murder of Australian nurse Yvonne Gilford, 55. The two, jailed in eastern Saudi Arabia since December 20, have said they were innocent.
Gilford was stabbed four times, battered with a hammer and smothered in her dormitory at the King Fahd military medical complex in the eastern oil city of Dhahran on December 11.

Under Sharia Islamic law they could face public beheading if found guilty of premeditated murder by a panel of three judges. Defendants have the right of appeal to two other five-judge panels before a final verdict is passed.
The defence statement said the court on Monday urged representatives of the Gilford family "to agree on a conciliatory settlement in principle against whoever turns to be the real killer..."
In the event of guilty verdicts, Gilford's family could spare the lives of the two and ask for financial recompensation known as blood money instead of the death sentence.

But the Gilford family on Monday confirmed their insistence on the death penalty, the defence statement said. Lawyers for the Gilford family, who have previously rejected a clemency appeal for the two, were not immediately available for comment.

The defence on Monday requested the invalidation of confessions by the two British nurses and said the court responded to a request to present an analytical memorandum on the issue by saying "this may not be needed. However, if it is the wish of your clients, then it is agreeable".

Saudi police have said the two confessed to the murder and the confessions were filed with the court. But the nurses later withdrew their confessions and one of them retracted a statement that she had a lesbian relationship with the victim.
But the worse case scenario presented by the defence said the three-judge court or a higher one "may consider the elements of guilt to be sufficient to establish guilt.
"But at the same time may disqualify the status of the Gilford family to demand the death penalty on the grounds of physical or mental factors and/or legal or religious factors."

The defence said it was unlikely the court would uphold the confessions but said if found guilty the Britons could "be sentenced to no more than five years in prison, and considering the poor quality of the evidence to probably a substantially lesser prison sentence."
